problem: The book has drilled that a Ring 3 program cannot touch hardware or reach a device's registers (ch1-kernel-p5, Fig BR.7's strip: only the kernel maps device ranges). quote: the kernel marks all of the parent's pages as read-only
problem: Three paragraphs earlier (p12), writing to a read-only page was the standard example of an invalid fault that ends in SIGSEGV. Nothing says how the kernel tells this copy-on-write write apart from an illegal one, so the reader cannot see why this fault leads to a copy and not a kill.

judge_fix: ch4-vm-p15: 'Instead the kernel marks all of the parent's pages as read-only in the page table, while keeping its own note that they are really writable, and shares them with the child. Only when one of them tries to write does a page fault occur, and because of that note the kernel copies that one page rather than killing the process.'

judge_fix: ch4-vm-p17, last sentence: 'A discard that fell between the copy and the write made the kernel, which was doing the write for the attacker, look the page up again and find the file's own page, so the write went into the file.'

quote: 2005 a first fix, later undone | 2007 Linux 2.6.22: flaw ships
problem: The timeline cannot be true in the order drawn: a 2005 fix for this race, then the flaw 'ships' two years later. The same claim makes 'nine years' in ch4-vm-p17 and the caption a lower bound, not the length.

judge_fix: Fig 4.11 labels: '2005 a fix, undone within days'; '2007 Linux 2.6.22: oldest kernel the advisories name'; bar 'nine years or more, in every kernel'; update the <desc> to match ('from Linux 2.6.22 in 2007, the oldest kernel the advisories name, the flaw is in every kernel, for nine years or more'). ch4-vm-p17: 'For at least nine years a race in Linux's copy-on-write code let any user write to read-only files...'. quote: The earliest multi-tasking systems were cooperative
problem: Time-sharing was preemptive from the start. CTSS was demonstrated in November 1961 and had a clock interrupt, a 200 ms quantum and a multilevel feedback queue (Wikipedia, Compatible_Time-Sharing_System). That is the MLFQ this chapter's own table lists. Ch1-kernel-p4 also says time-sharing used a hardware timer. Cooperative multitasking belongs to the personal-computer systems this paragraph names (Mac OS to 9, 16-bit Windows), not to the earliest systems. Together with p3's 'Modern systems are preemptive', it leaves the reader believing preemption came later.
fix: 'Many early personal-computer systems were _cooperative_: each running program voluntarily yielded control...'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compatible_Time-Sharing_System (clock interrupt, 200 ms quantum, MLFQ, 1961).
reason: CTSS (1961) had a clock interrupt and a 200 ms quantum with a multilevel feedback queue (Wikipedia, Compatible_Time-Sharing_System), and ch1-kernel-p4 says time-sharing used a hardware timer. The paragraph's own examples (Mac OS 9, 16-bit Windows) are personal-computer systems, so 'earliest multi-tasking systems' is wrong and, with p3's 'Modern systems are preemptive', implies preemption came later.
judge_fix: ch4-scheduling-p2: 'Many early personal-computer systems were _cooperative_: each running program voluntarily yielded control back to the scheduler when it had nothing useful to do. Mac OS through version 9 worked this way, as did 16-bit Windows. ...' (rest unchanged).

File contents go straight to their home blocks. The figure's own strip says so two screens later. 'Each change lands whole or not at all' is likewise true only of the structural (metadata) changes.

Source: §4g Fig 4.13 row; ext4 data=ordered default (docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/ext4.html).
reason: p9 says 'every intended modification is written first', but Fig 4.13's strip and UNDER.md §4g (Pass 28 row) say ext4 data=ordered and NTFS journal metadata only. The prose brings back the corrected error and contradicts the figure two screens later.
judge_fix: ch4-fs-p9: '...is the **journal**, a small, dedicated region of the disk where each change to the filesystem's structure (inodes, free-block maps, directories) is written _first_, then applied to the main filesystem. Each such change in the journal ends with a commit record, written last; after a crash, the kernel replays the changes that have one and discards those that do not. Each change lands whole or not at all, ...'. Source: §4g Fig 4.13 row; docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/ext4.html (data=ordered default).

This sentence says the opposite in the chapter that is about the kernel.

quote: so work that must respond quickly runs on time rather than merely fairly
problem: EEVDF's deadlines are virtual (eligible time plus requested slice over weight), not wall-clock deadlines. EEVDF stays a fair-share scheduler: tasks that ask for shorter slices are picked sooner, but no deadline is guaranteed (docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html). 'Runs on time rather than merely fairly' implies real-time behaviour that trades away fairness, which p12 then denies for general-purpose schedulers. Fig 4.4's strip repeats it: 'so latency-sensitive work runs on time'.
fix: p5: '...but gives every task a virtual deadline set by the slice it asks for, so a task that asks for short slices gets the CPU sooner without taking more than its share.' Fig 4.4 strip: '...picks the eligible task with the earliest virtual deadline, so tasks that ask for short slices are served sooner.' Source: docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html.
reason: Checked docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html: EEVDF aims for equal sharing among equal-priority tasks, picks the eligible task with the earliest virtual deadline, and favours tasks that request shorter slices. It gives no latency bound. 'Runs on time rather than merely fairly' implies real-time behaviour, which p12 then says general-purpose schedulers do not give. Fig 4.4's strip repeats it.
judge_fix: p5 end: '...Linux's default is CFS's successor *EEVDF* (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First), which keeps the same bookkeeping but gives every task a virtual deadline set by the slice it asks for, so a task that asks for short slices gets the CPU sooner without taking more than its share.' Fig 4.4 strip: '...picks the eligible task with the earliest virtual deadline, so tasks that ask for short slices are served sooner.' Source: docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html.

quote: For the simplest queue, one server with random arrivals, W is exactly 1/(μ − λ).
problem: The formula needs random (exponential) service times as well as random arrivals: that is what M/M/1 means. With random arrivals and fixed service times (M/D/1), W at 95% load is 10.5 service times, not 20. Fig 4.6's strip has the same gap: '(random arrivals, one server, called M/M/1)'.
fix: p10: 'For the simplest queue, one server with random arrivals and random service times, W is exactly 1/(μ − λ).' Fig 4.6 strip: '(random arrivals and service times, one server, called M/M/1)'.
reason: 1/(mu - lambda) is the M/M/1 result and needs random service times as well as random arrivals. With fixed service times (M/D/1) the time at 95% load is about 10.5 service times, not 20. The figure strip names 'M/M/1' but does not say service times are random.
judge_fix: p10: 'For the simplest queue, one server with random arrivals and random service times, W is exactly 1/(μ − λ).' Fig 4.6 strip: '(random arrivals and service times, one server, called M/M/1)'.

quote: 10 requests a second, each inside for 2 seconds, keeps 20 inside at any moment

problem: True of PID namespaces, which the second half of the sentence illustrates, but stated for all namespaces. quote: gives a new process (or, for PID, the caller's next children) a fresh namespace
problem: This is right for clone(), which starts a new process in the new namespace. It is wrong for unshare(), which moves the calling process itself into the new namespace and creates no new process. The PID exception applies to unshare(): there, only the caller's next children enter it (unshare(2)).
fix: '`clone()` with a flag such as `CLONE_NEWPID` starts a new process in a fresh namespace, which its children inherit; `unshare()` moves the caller itself (for PID, only its next children).' Source: man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/unshare.2.html.
reason: Per unshare(2), unshare() moves the calling process into the new namespace and creates no new process. For CLONE_NEWPID only the caller's next children enter it. clone() starts a new process in the new namespace. The strip's sentence blends the two calls.
judge_fix: fig-4-20 strip 'Making one': '`clone()` with a flag such as `CLONE_NEWPID` starts a new process in a fresh namespace; `unshare()` moves the caller itself into one (for PID, only its next children). Children inherit the namespace.' Source: man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/unshare.2.html.

When a virtual page has no physical page in RAM (it has never been used, was moved to disk to free RAM, or belongs to a file mapped into memory but not yet read), the kernel marks its entry invalid, and touching it makes the MMU raise a hardware exception called a **page fault**. The kernel's page-fault handler decides what to do." problem: chBridge-timer-p1 and p2 already teach cooperative multitasking, the program that never yields and freezes the machine, preemption and the per-core hardware timer, and ch1-kernel-p4 covers the timer too. p2 and p3 teach cooperative and preemptive again as fresh italic definitions.
